day-1.t: Day 1 — A profile that survives the ten-second read

b.v: Today's goal

v: Write a profile title that names one job
Rewrite the first two lines of your overview
Set your rate to a real number, not a guess

b.v: About 20 minutes. Open Upwork and read your own profile on a phone, as a client would.
On Upwork a client does not shop. They compare four or five profiles for one job and stop reading fast. Your profile is not a CV. It is an answer to one question: can this person do my job this week?
1) The title names the job, not the person
Your title appears in search results next to your photo. Use the words a client would type when posting the job.

v: weak = Hardworking freelancer, available 24/7
strong = Excel data cleanup and monthly reporting for small businesses
weak = Expert with many skills
strong = Urdu to English translation of legal and business documents

b.v: 2) First two lines of the overview
Only the beginning shows before the client clicks more. Say the problem you solve, for whom, and one proof point. No greeting, no years of experience, no passion.
3) Your rate is a signal

A rate far below everyone else reads as a beginner or a risk. A rate far above reads as a mistake. Start near the lower middle of what you see for your job type, then raise it after your first few contracts.
Do not set your rate at the lowest possible number to win the first job. Clients who choose only on price are the ones who ask for the most changes, and the rate is very hard to raise later.
Practice
Rewrite your title and the first two lines of your overview on paper. Read them out loud. If a stranger could not say what job you do and for whom, cut words until they can.

day-2.t: Day 2 — A portfolio with no clients yet

b.v: Today's goal

v: Build three portfolio pieces without a single client
Write the one line that frames each piece
Mark samples honestly so nobody feels tricked

b.v: About 25 minutes. You need the files you already made for practice.
No client will hand a paid job to someone with nothing to show. The way out is not a lie. It is a set of small, honest samples that prove the exact work you are selling.
1) Make the sample you wish you had been given
Take a real, public problem and solve it. Do not invent a fake brand with a fake logo and call it client work. Build the thing itself: the cleaned sheet, the translation, the edited clip, the report.

v: A messy public dataset, cleaned and turned into a one-page summary
A ten-page Urdu document translated, with a glossary of terms you chose
A short video edited from free stock footage
A monthly reporting template with dummy numbers, clearly labelled

b.v: 2) Frame each piece in three lines
A sample without context looks like a hobby. Three lines turn it into evidence: the problem, what you did, the result.

@Portfolio caption
Problem: a 900-row sales export with duplicate entries and four date formats.
What I did: removed 61 duplicates, standardised the dates, built a one-page monthly summary.
Result: the shop owner could see which two products were losing money.
3) Say what is a sample
Put a small honest note such as sample project built to show my process on each piece that was not paid client work. Clients respect it, and it protects you from a dispute later.
Do not copy someone else's portfolio, and do not claim a project you did not do. Clients check, and a false portfolio is grounds for removal from the platform.
Practice
Build one piece tonight with free or public material, then write its three-line caption. Two more pieces will follow on later days; one good piece beats five empty placeholders.
Today's goal

v: Understand when a second, specialised profile helps
Choose the specialisation from your own evidence
Keep one main profile strong instead of two weak ones

b.v: About 20 minutes. Look at the jobs you have saved or applied to in the last month.
Upwork lets you hold more than one profile under some conditions, and clients can find you through each one. The point is not more profiles. The point is being the obvious match for one kind of job.
1) Specialise on the work you can prove
Look at your applications and your samples. Which job type appears again and again? That is your specialisation, not the one that sounds most impressive.

v: The job type you have applied to most often
The sample you finished fastest and best
The job where you already know the client's vocabulary
The job you could describe to a beginner in five minutes

b.v: 2) One profile, one promise
A specialised profile speaks to one buyer. The title, the overview, the portfolio and the skills all point at the same job. If a section could belong to any freelancer, rewrite it.

Rewrite a profile for one specialisation:|Title: the job plus the client type|Overview first two lines: the problem you solve, in their words|Skills: only the ones used in that job|Portfolio: only pieces from that job|Rate: the rate for that job, not your average
Do not create a second profile to escape a low score or a bad review. That is treated as circumventing the system and can cost you both accounts.
3) When a second profile is worth it
Only when the second job is genuinely different work with a different client, and the first profile is already earning. Two half-finished profiles rank worse than one complete one.

v: Worth it: translation and Excel cleanup, different clients, both active
Not worth it: two profiles that both say I can do anything
Not worth it: a second profile made last week and never touched

b.v: Practice
Write the one job you will be known for in the next ninety days. Then edit your title, skills and portfolio so that nothing on the profile points at a different job.

day-4.t: Day 4 — Proposals that answer the brief

b.v: Today's goal

v: Open with the client's problem, not with yourself
Answer every requirement in the post
End with one small, easy next step

b.v: About 25 minutes. Pick one real open job and write the proposal in full.

A client posting a job reads many proposals that all begin with I am an expert with five years of experience. Those are skipped. The proposals that get replies sound like a person who read the post and already started thinking about the work.
1) The first two lines do the work
Name the specific thing in the post that you understand. This proves you read it, and it separates you from the copy-paste crowd in one sentence.

v: weak = Dear Sir, I am the best choice for this job
strong = You have 300 product photos that need the background removed and the file names matched to your SKU list
weak = I have excellent communication skills
strong = Your sheet breaks because the dates are in three formats — that is the first thing I would fix

b.v: 2) Answer the brief line by line
Most posts contain a list. Go through it and answer each point. A short bullet list that matches their list is more persuasive than three paragraphs of praise.

@Proposal skeleton
Your post asks for 300 photos with clean backgrounds and SKU file names before Friday.

How I would do it
- Cut out and clean each image, keeping the shadow soft
- Name each file exactly as your list shows, e.g. SKU-1042.jpg
- Send a spreadsheet noting any SKU that was missing from the folder

Timeline: the first 100 by Wednesday, all 300 by Thursday night, so you have Friday to check.

One question: should the images be square or keep their original shape?

Do not send the same proposal to ten jobs with the first line unchanged. Clients see the same template repeatedly, and Upwork tracks how many proposals turn into conversations. A few careful proposals beat fifty copied ones.
3) Close with one question, not a paragraph
A question gives the client an easy reason to reply, and a reply starts a conversation. Ask something small that you genuinely need to know.

v: Which format do you need the final file in?
Is the deadline fixed or can it move by one day?
Should I match the style of your existing documents?

b.v: Practice
Write one complete proposal for a real open job today, in the skeleton above, under 200 words. Read it once and delete every sentence that is about you rather than about their job.

day-5.t: Day 5 — Connects, and how to spend them

b.v: Today's goal

v: Understand what a Connect is and what it costs
Build a weekly plan for spending them
Stop applying to jobs you cannot win

b.v: About 15 minutes. Check the current price of Connects and the free allowance at the time of writing, because both change.
A Connect is the credit you spend to send a proposal or to boost one. Free Connects are limited and buying more costs real money, so every proposal is a small purchase. Treat it like one.
1) Read the job before you spend
Most wasted Connects go to jobs that were never going to hire you: too many proposals already, a client with no payment history, or a budget that cannot cover the work.

v: How many proposals are already there, and how long ago was it posted
Does the client have a verified payment method and past hires
Is the budget realistic for the work described
Does the post describe the job clearly, or is it one vague line

b.v: 2) Spend on the jobs you can actually win
Your best chance is a job that matches your samples exactly, has few proposals, and was posted within the last day. Save your Connects for those and skip the rest.

Weekly Connects plan:|Monday: shortlist five jobs that match your samples|Remove any job older than two days or already crowded|Write full proposals for the best two|Keep the rest of your Connects for jobs posted later in the week|Write down what you spent and what came back
Do not boost a proposal for a job you are not a strong match for. A boost only moves a weak proposal higher up the list, where the client still reads it and still says no.
3) Track the return
Connects are only worth it if they turn into conversations. Count replies, not proposals sent. If ten proposals bring zero replies, the problem is your opening lines, not your budget.

v: Replies per ten proposals is your real number
Change one thing at a time: the first line, then the price, then the timeline
Stop applying to a job type that never replies

b.v: Practice
Shortlist five open jobs and score each one from 1 to 5 for fit with your samples. Only write proposals for the two scoring highest, and note how many Connects each one costs.

day-6.t: Day 6 — Interviews that turn into contracts

b.v: Today's goal

v: Prepare for the first call in fifteen minutes
Ask the four questions that prevent a bad job
Send a short written summary after the call

b.v: About 20 minutes. Do this before your next interview, not after.
An interview is not an exam. The client is checking two things: can you do it, and will working with you be easy. Both are answered by preparation and by asking good questions.
1) Prepare three things only
You do not need a script. You need the file, the plan and the price.

v: One sample that looks like their job
A three-step plan for their work, in order
A price and a delivery date you can hold to

b.v: 2) Ask the four questions
These four prevent almost every later dispute. Ask them in the chat or the call, and write the answers down.

v: What does done look like for you?
Who checks the work, and how many rounds of changes are normal?
What is the deadline, and is anything waiting on your side?
Is this a one-time job or something you need every month?

b.v: Do not promise a deadline you have not checked against your other work. A missed date in the first contract is much worse than a later date agreed at the start.
3) Send the summary the same day
A short written summary after the call does three things: it proves you listened, it creates a record, and it moves the client towards starting.

@After-interview message
Thank you for the call. To confirm what we agreed:
- Scope: 300 product photos, background removed, named by SKU
- First 100 by Wednesday, all 300 by Thursday night
- Two rounds of changes included
- Price: as discussed, through a funded milestone before I start

If that is right, send the folder and I will begin the same day.
Practice
Write your four questions in your notes app and your after-call summary template next to them. Then say your three-step plan out loud for one real job, in under one minute.

day-7.t: Day 7 — Milestones, escrow and getting paid

b.v: Today's goal

v: Understand what escrow actually protects
Break a job into milestones that release on delivery
Never start work on an unfunded contract

b.v: About 20 minutes. Read the contract terms on your next job before you accept it.
Escrow means the client's money is held by the platform before you work. It is the reason you can work for a stranger in another country. If the money is not in escrow, you are working on a promise.
1) Funded first, then work
A milestone shows as funded when the client has paid into it. Check that before you open the file. A client who says the payment is coming is a client who has not paid.

v: Contract started with a funded milestone = safe to begin
Contract started with no funds = ask for the milestone to be funded first
Client asks to pay after delivery = refuse politely and keep the work in escrow

b.v: 2) Split big jobs into small milestones
One large milestone puts all the risk at the end. Three small ones keep money moving and show the client progress, which reduces Nervous messages.

Split a Rs 60,000 job:|Milestone 1 — first 100 files, released on delivery|Milestone 2 — next 100 files|Milestone 3 — final 100 files plus the summary sheet|Write the release condition in the milestone itself

Never accept payment outside the platform to save the fee. You lose escrow protection, you lose the dispute option, and it breaks the terms you agreed to. Check the current fee at the time of writing and price your work with it in mind.
3) Submit properly, not just by message
Use the submit button for the milestone when the work is done. A file dropped in the chat is not a submission, and the clock that protects you does not start.

v: Attach the file to the milestone submission
Write what is included and what you checked
Ask for the release in one clear line
Keep a copy of everything you delivered

b.v: Practice
Take one job you are discussing and split it into three milestones with a clear release condition for each. Write the split in the chat so the client agrees before the contract starts.

day-8.t: Day 8 — Scope creep without the argument

b.v: Today's goal

v: Spot scope creep in the first message that hints at it
Use one sentence that adds work without sounding rude
Keep the client and the money

b.v: About 20 minutes. Think of a job where you did extra work for free.
Scope creep is small extra requests that arrive one at a time. Each one looks harmless. Together they turn a two-day job into two weeks, and the client never realises they asked.
1) The early signs
The first free extra is always small and always sounds reasonable. That is the moment to set the pattern, not after the fifth one.

v: Can you also just add a summary sheet?
While you are in there, can you fix the formatting on the old files too?
One quick call to explain it?
My colleague wants a second version in a different style

b.v: 2) One sentence, three parts
Acknowledge, separate, price. Never say no without offering a way forward, and never say yes to unpaid work to avoid an awkward moment.

@Scope reply
Happy to add the summary sheet. That is outside the current milestone, so I can do it as a small add-on for the price we agreed, delivered the next day. Should I add it now?
3) Put the boundary in writing at the start
The cheapest protection is one line in the first message, before the contract. It sets the expectation while everyone is friendly.

v: This price covers 300 photos, two rounds of changes and one delivery format.
Extra formats or extra rounds are a small add-on and I will always quote before doing them.
New files after delivery are a new milestone.

b.v: Do not do the extra work first and then ask to be paid. Once the work is delivered the client has no reason to agree to a new price, and you will resent the job and show it in the next message.
Practice
Write your scope sentence in your own words and save it. Then look at your last job and write down every extra you did for free, with the hours it took.
Today's goal

v: Choose the right contract type for the job
Log hours honestly and describe them clearly
Know when to switch from hourly to fixed

b.v: About 20 minutes. Check how the hourly protection works on the platform at the time of writing; the rules and weekly limits change.
Hourly pays for your time. Fixed pays for a result. Choosing the wrong one is how good freelancers end up working for half their rate, or arguing about a bill nobody can prove.
1) Fixed price fits clear, repeatable jobs
If you can describe the deliverable in one sentence and count it, use fixed. The client knows the cost, you know the work, and the dispute is about the file, not the clock.

v: 300 photos, 20 pages translated, one cleaned sheet, one report
Good when you are fast and know the exact steps
Bad when the client cannot say what they want yet

b.v: 2) Hourly fits unknown or changing work
Research, ongoing support, and anything where the client keeps discovering new needs belongs on the clock. On hourly, track time as you work, with a short note on what you did.

Log the hour properly:|Start the timer when you begin, not at the end of the day|Write the note while it is fresh, for example cleaned 80 rows and matched totals|Add the file you worked on in the note|Stop the timer for long breaks and say so in the message
Do not log hours you did not work, and do not describe a whole day as research. Clients read the notes before paying, and one inflated entry makes every later entry look doubtful.
3) Switching when the job changes
If a fixed job keeps growing, finish the current milestone and then propose the change in writing, with numbers.

v: The work so far matches the milestone. The new part is about six hours, so I suggest a second milestone for it.
If the requests will keep coming, hourly may be simpler for both of us. Which do you prefer?

b.v: Practice
Write the job types you would only do hourly and the ones you would only do fixed. Then write your time-note format in one line you can reuse on every hourly contract.

day-10.t: Day 10 — End well, and get hired again

b.v: Today's goal

v: Close a contract so the feedback is good
Understand the Job Success Score in plain words
Ask for the next job without being awkward

b.v: About 20 minutes. Open your last completed contract and read the feedback you left.
Most freelancers treat the end of a contract as the finish line. It is actually the cheapest place to find the next job, because the client already trusts you.
1) Close it properly
Deliver, confirm in writing, ask for the milestone to be released, then close the contract. Do not leave finished contracts open for months.

v: Send the final file with a one-line summary of what changed
Ask the client to confirm it is complete
Ask for the milestone release, then close the contract
Leave honest, specific feedback for the client

b.v: 2) The Job Success Score in plain words

The Job Success Score, usually called JSS, is a number the platform gives you from your contract history. It is built from client feedback, including feedback clients give privately, plus things like completed contracts, on-time work and long relationships. The exact formula is not published, so do not chase it directly.

v: Finish what you start, and avoid cancellations
Keep the same client for repeat work
Deliver before the deadline, not on it
Keep every payment and message inside the platform

b.v: Bad private feedback counts even when the client leaves five public stars. The way to protect your score is a short message before delivery: is anything missing? That one question prevents most surprises.
3) Ask for the next job
The best moment to ask is right after a good delivery. Keep it to two lines and make it easy to say yes.

@Repeat work message
I am glad the sheet worked. Two things I can also take off your desk: the monthly version of this file, and the supplier list that still has duplicates. Should I quote for either of them?
Practice

Write your closing message and your repeat-work message, then save both. Send the repeat-work message to one past client or, if you have none yet, write the version you will send after your first delivery.
